analysis.one_liner: Cuts taxes for oil and gas producers and guarantees them an $18 minimum price per barrel.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, was referred to three House committees, and died in subcommittees without a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cut federal taxes for domestic oil and gas producers, especially operators of low-output 'stripper' wells, by raising their depletion deduction and shielding them from the alternative minimum tax. It would have guaranteed those producers an $18-per-barrel price floor by requiring refiners to buy from them and charging importers a fee into a government fund, and it would have directed the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to buy stripper well oil. It also would have lifted remaining natural gas wellhead price controls and told banking regulators to loosen rules on lenders stuck with troubled energy loans.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic oil and gas producers, above all operators of stripper wells, would gain through larger tax deductions, exemption from the alternative minimum tax, and a guaranteed $18 minimum price with civil and criminal penalties for refiners who pay less. Natural gas producers would gain from the removal of wellhead price controls. Banks and thrifts holding troubled energy loans would gain from relaxed rescheduling and capital rules.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the percentage depletion deduction for stripper well production from 15% to 27.5% and removes the net income limit on oil and gas depletion, letting producers shelter more income.
Repeals the treatment of intangible drilling costs and percentage depletion as tax preference items under the alternative minimum tax, reducing producers' minimum tax bills.
Creates a deduction for crude oil producers of 100% of losses on independent producer oil and 80% on other domestic crude, with a six-year carryback of qualified losses against past taxes.

Requires the President to set a regulation imposing an $18 per barrel minimum wellhead price on purchases from domestic independent producers, with refiners paying any savings into a Refiners' Blending Surcharge Fund and importers paying a fee on cheaper imported products; half the fund goes to deficit reduction.
Directs banking regulators to grant lenders with energy-related loans greater flexibility in rescheduling or marking down troubled loans and to ease bank capital requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers of gasoline, diesel, and heating oil would bear the cost of the $18 price floor and the importer fee, which raise the price of crude and petroleum products above world market levels. The Treasury would collect less revenue from the expanded producer tax breaks, and the Strategic Petroleum Reserve purchasing mandate would direct federal dollars to stripper well oil.
analysis.who_pays_short: Motorists and energy consumers, plus taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The $18 minimum price and importer surcharge would force Americans to pay more for gasoline and other petroleum products than the world market price, functioning like a tax on consumers paid to domestic producers.

The expanded depletion deductions, alternative minimum tax repeal, and loss deductions would reduce federal revenue, and the bill itself acknowledges the budget deficit by routing half of the surcharge fund to deficit reduction.

Easing bank capital requirements and allowing lenders to avoid marking down troubled energy loans would leave weak loans on bank books at a time when deposit insurance funds were already strained, shifting risk toward the government backstop.
A price floor insulates producers from competition and keeps higher-cost wells running, which economists generally view as keeping resources tied up in unprofitable production.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated case was energy security: keeping marginal domestic wells producing so the country depends less on imports, and refilling the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to 750 million barrels. But the bill would achieve this by making consumers pay above-market prices and by cutting producers' taxes, with the bill itself devoting half of a new surcharge fund to deficit reduction — an acknowledgment that the tax provisions cost revenue. The bank provisions loosen capital rules during a period of deposit-insurance stress. The security benefit was real but was being purchased largely at the expense of energy consumers and the Treasury.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees the day it was introduced, passed down to two subcommittees in March 1989, and never came back out — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Wes Watkins of Oklahoma introduced the Secure Energy Supply Act of 1989 on February 9, 1989.
It was referred jointly the same day to three committees: Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs.
On February 27, 1989 it was referred to the Energy and Power Subcommittee, and on March 15, 1989 to the Financial Institutions Subcommittee; those were the last actions of any kind.
No further action was taken before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, so the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Energy consumers and the Treasury came out ahead, because the $18 oil price floor, importer surcharge, and expanded producer tax breaks never became law. Domestic oil and gas producers lost the chance at the guaranteed price and tax benefits.

for.name: Rep. Wes Watkins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it jointly to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Banking committees.

against.name: House Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Banking Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 9, 1989 and took no action beyond passing it to subcommittees; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record beyond the Democratic sponsor.

industries.industry: Domestic oil and gas producers (especially stripper well operators)
industries.note: The bill would hand them a larger depletion deduction, alternative minimum tax relief, and a government-enforced $18 per barrel minimum price with civil and criminal penalties for refiners who pay less. The money for that guaranteed price comes out of what consumers pay at the pump.

Refiners would be forced to keep buying crude from domestic independent producers at a minimum of $18 a barrel and to pay any savings from cheaper oil into a federal fund, raising their input costs. Those costs would tend to be passed on in fuel prices.

The bill removes the remaining Natural Gas Policy Act wellhead price controls and repeals the President's standby authority to reimpose them, freeing producers to charge market rates. Consumers could face higher gas prices, though deregulation also removed a layer of price distortion.

industries.industry: Banks and thrifts holding energy loans
industries.note: Regulators would be directed to let lenders reschedule or avoid marking down troubled energy loans and to ease capital requirements. Avoiding markdowns keeps weak loans on the books and shifts the risk onto the deposit insurance funds standing behind those institutions.

Importers would pay a fee equal to the gap between the domestic rack price and their import price, depositing it into the Refiners' Blending Surcharge Fund. The fee raises the cost of imported products and pushes consumers toward more expensive domestic supply.
